newsitem.title: CANADA: Ukraine's prime minister says he is not corrupt.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's prime minister says he is not corrupt.

text.p: Ukrainian Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko said on Friday there was corruption in his country that he was trying to root out but stressed he was not personally involved.
"We have corruption in Ukraine as in any other country," said Lazarenko, standing at Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien's side after bilateral talks.
"Whether I am implicated in all these publications in the mass media, I'm telling you unambiguously I am not implicated," he told reporters through an interpreter.

Lazarenko, trying to drum up business during a five-day visit to Canada, was confronted with a front-page article this week in Toronto's influential Globe and Mail newspaper about allegations of corruption.

It cited a New York Times article quoting Western intelligence reports estimating that Lazarenko gained about $260 million from his unofficial involvement in United Energy Systems, which had a license to import cheap Russian gas.

The Globe said the president's staff insisted he had received "not a single cent" from business activities because such activities were forbidden by law. He declared an official income of only a few thousand dollars last year, it said.

U.S. Vice President Al Gore stated publicly during a visit to Washington by Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma last month that "all possible efforts must be focused on eliminating corruption from public life."
Chretien would not comment on allegations of corruption, saying only: "He is the prime minister, and we have good relations with Ukraine, and I was happy to receive him."

Lazarenko said: "It was the Lazarenko government which was very firm in introducing harsh new measures to combat corruption." He said earlier at the National Press Club that corruption in Ukraine was exaggerated by political opponents trying to undermine his government ahead of elections expected in nine months.

Lazarenko will spend the next few days travelling across Canada to promote trade and investment. About 500,000 people of Ukrainian descent live in Canada, the first Western country to recognise Ukraine after its declaration of independence in December 1991.
